questions.question: Explain what a rural settlement is and describe the factors that influenced the site of early settlements.
questions.expected_answer: A settlement is any place where people live. Rural settlements are small settlements in the countryside where most people work in primary activities that take resources directly from nature, such as farming, mining, forestry and fishing, and where there are few services, so people travel to towns for hospitals, banks and larger shops. Site is the land a settlement is built on; important site factors were a reliable water supply, flat or gently sloping land, fertile soil, protection from flooding on slightly higher ground near rivers, shelter from wind, safety from attack and nearby building materials such as wood, stone, clay or grass. Situation is the settlement's position in relation to roads, rivers, other settlements and resources.

questions.question: Describe the isolated farmstead, the hamlet and the village, and explain the settlement hierarchy.
questions.expected_answer: An isolated farmstead is a single farmhouse with outbuildings and workers' houses standing alone on a farm, with no public services, typical of large commercial farms in the Karoo, Northern Cape or Free State and producing a dispersed pattern. A hamlet is a small group of houses, a few to around twenty households, with very few or no services, such as clusters of family homesteads in rural KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape. A village is larger, from a few hundred to a few thousand people, with basic services such as a primary school, shop, church and perhaps a clinic or police station, often nucleated, such as Paternoster or Genadendal. The settlement hierarchy ranks settlements by size and services: moving up, there are fewer settlements, each with more people and more and higher-order services, and settlements of the same rank are further apart. Low-order services such as a small shop are found in villages; high-order services such as specialist hospitals and universities only in large towns and cities.

questions.question: Describe how farming, mining, forestry and fishing support rural settlements in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Commercial farming grows crops and livestock for profit, such as maize in the Free State and North West, sugar cane in KwaZulu-Natal, fruit and wine in the Western Cape, citrus in Limpopo and Mpumalanga and sheep and cattle in the Karoo; subsistence farming in the former homelands produces food for households. Mining creates planned settlements near coal in Mpumalanga, platinum in North West and Limpopo, iron ore near Kathu and Sishen and diamonds in the Northern Cape and on the West Coast; these may decline when minerals run out. Forestry villages house workers on pine and eucalyptus plantations in wetter, cooler parts of Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape and near Knysna's forests, with sawmills nearby. Fishing villages such as Paternoster, Lamberts Bay and Port Nolloth grew on the West Coast because the cold Benguela Current supports rich fish stocks. Many rural settlements also rely on tourism, grants and remittances.
